glossary.definition: Basic functions like nutrition, respiration, transport, and excretion that maintain life.
Process of obtaining and using food for growth, repair, and energy.
Synthesis of food in green plants using CO₂, water, and sunlight.
Organism makes its own food from inorganic substances.
Organism depends on ready-made organic food from other organisms.
Release of energy from food inside cells, often using oxygen.
Respiration using oxygen; complete breakdown of glucose in mitochondria.
Respiration without oxygen; partial breakdown with less ATP.
Vascular tissue transporting water and minerals upward in plants.
Vascular tissue transporting food (sucrose) in plants.
Removal of harmful metabolic wastes from the body.
Structural and functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine.

concepts.name: What are life processes?
concepts.simple_answer: Life processes are the basic functions performed by living organisms to maintain life — nutrition, respiration, transport, excretion, and more.
concepts.why: NCERT Ch 5 opens with maintenance of life.
concepts.example: Even when not growing, your body still needs energy and repair.
concepts.remember: Living things must carry out life processes continuously.
concepts.common_confusion: Being alive is not just about moving — plants also perform life processes.

concepts.name: Why maintenance is needed
concepts.simple_answer: Living organisms need maintenance even when not growing because body cells are constantly being damaged and need repair.
concepts.why: Explains why life processes never stop.
concepts.example: Skin cells replace themselves; muscles need ATP daily.
concepts.remember: Maintenance needs energy from outside or from food.
concepts.common_confusion: Sleeping does not mean life processes stop.

concepts.name: Molecular movement and life
concepts.simple_answer: All living organisms need to move molecules across their body for life processes — even plants without visible movement.
concepts.why: Bridge from diffusion to transport systems.
concepts.example: O₂ must reach every cell; CO₂ must leave.
concepts.remember: Life needs controlled movement of substances.
concepts.common_confusion: Plants don't move but still transport water and food.

concepts.name: Diffusion — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Diffusion is the movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration until evenly spread.
concepts.example: Perfume spreading in a room.
concepts.remember: No energy needed for simple diffusion.
concepts.common_confusion: Diffusion works only over very short distances.

concepts.name: Diffusion in unicellular organisms
concepts.simple_answer: In unicellular organisms, the entire surface is in direct contact with the environment — diffusion alone is enough.
concepts.why: Contrast with multicellular need for transport.
concepts.example: Amoeba absorbs food and O₂ by diffusion through cell surface.
concepts.remember: Small size + large surface area → diffusion works.

concepts.name: Diffusion insufficient in multicellular organisms
concepts.simple_answer: In large multicellular organisms most cells are not in direct contact with the environment — diffusion alone is too slow.
concepts.example: Your innermost cells cannot get O₂ by diffusion from skin.
concepts.remember: Special transport systems are needed in large bodies.
concepts.common_confusion: Diffusion still works at cell level after delivery.

concepts.name: What makes something alive?
concepts.simple_answer: We decide something is alive if it shows molecular movement needed for repair and maintenance — not just visible movement.
concepts.example: A seed is alive though it looks inactive; it respires slowly.
concepts.remember: Visible movement alone is not enough to prove life.
concepts.common_confusion: Viruses are debated — they need a host to reproduce.

concepts.name: Outside raw materials
concepts.simple_answer: Living organisms take in raw materials from outside: carbon-based food/CO₂, water, and inorganic salts.
concepts.example: Plants: CO₂ + water + minerals. Animals: food + water + salts.
concepts.remember: Carbon sources, water, and minerals from environment.
concepts.common_confusion: Autotrophs build food; heterotrophs eat ready-made food.

concepts.name: Energy for life processes
concepts.simple_answer: Outside materials are used to build body structure and to provide energy for life processes.
concepts.why: Links nutrition to all other processes.
concepts.example: Glucose from food powers muscle contraction and nerve signals.
concepts.common_confusion: Energy is stored in chemical bonds of food molecules.

concepts.name: Chapter 5 roadmap
concepts.simple_answer: Ch 5 covers nutrition, respiration, transport, and excretion in plants and humans.
concepts.example: Activities 5.1–5.8 support each section.

concepts.name: Nutrition — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Nutrition is the process of obtaining and using food for growth, repair, and energy.
concepts.why: First major life process in Ch 5.
concepts.example: Eating breakfast provides glucose for the school day.
concepts.common_confusion: Nutrition is not the same as digestion alone.

concepts.name: Autotrophic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Autotrophic nutrition: organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances like CO₂ and water.
concepts.example: Plants use sunlight to build starch.
concepts.remember: Make food from inorganic raw materials.
concepts.common_confusion: Autotrophs are producers in food chains.

concepts.name: Heterotrophic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Heterotrophic nutrition: organism depends on ready-made organic food from other organisms.
concepts.example: Humans eat plants and animals; cannot make glucose from CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: All animals are heterotrophs.

concepts.name: Saprotrophic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Saprotrophic nutrition: organisms feed on dead and decaying organic matter (e.g. fungi).
concepts.example: Mushrooms on rotting logs.
concepts.common_confusion: Saprotrophs secrete enzymes outside then absorb.

concepts.name: Parasitic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Parasitic nutrition: organism lives on or in a host and derives food at host's expense.
concepts.example: Tapeworm in intestine absorbs digested food.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all parasites kill the host immediately.

concepts.name: Holozoic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Holozoic nutrition: complex food is ingested and then digested inside the body.
concepts.example: Amoeba engulfs food; humans chew and swallow.

concepts.name: Modes of nutrition summary
concepts.simple_answer: Main modes: autotrophic (plants) and heterotrophic (animals, fungi) with subtypes saprotrophic, parasitic, holozoic.
concepts.example: Compare amoeba (holozoic) vs mushroom (saprotrophic).
concepts.common_confusion: Autotrophic vs heterotrophic is the primary split.

concepts.name: Enzymes in nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up breakdown of complex food into absorbable simple molecules.
concepts.example: Amylase breaks starch to sugar in saliva.
concepts.remember: Enzymes work at body temperature; are specific.
concepts.common_confusion: Enzymes are not used up in the reaction.

concepts.name: Nutrition in green plants — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Green plants are autotrophs: leaves trap light; roots absorb water and minerals.
concepts.example: Leaf = food factory; root = water and mineral uptake.
concepts.remember: Photosynthesis in leaves; absorption by roots.

concepts.name: Nutrition in animals — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Animals are heterotrophs: ingest food, digest it, absorb nutrients, and remove undigested waste.
concepts.example: Human alimentary canal is about 9 metres long.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants synthesise food (glucose) using CO₂, water, and sunlight.
concepts.example: Leaves produce O₂ we breathe.
concepts.common_confusion: Photosynthesis occurs only in green parts with chlorophyll.

concepts.name: Raw materials for photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Plants need CO₂ from air (through stomata), water from soil (through roots), and sunlight.
concepts.example: Stomata take in CO₂; xylem brings water to leaf.
concepts.common_confusion: Minerals from soil are needed for chlorophyll but not in the main equation.

concepts.name: Chlorophyll role
concepts.simple_answer: Chlorophyll in chloroplasts traps solar energy needed to convert CO₂ and water into glucose.
concepts.example: Without chlorophyll, photosynthesis cannot occur.
concepts.remember: Green pigment in chloroplasts absorbs light.
concepts.common_confusion: Other pigments exist but chlorophyll is primary.

concepts.name: Chloroplast location
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in mesophyll cells of leaves where chloroplasts are abundant.
concepts.example: Upper and lower mesophyll packed with chloroplasts.
concepts.remember: Leaf is the main photosynthetic organ.

concepts.name: Stomata and gas exchange
concepts.simple_answer: Stomata are tiny pores on leaf surface; they allow CO₂ intake and O₂ release during photosynthesis.
concepts.example: Guard cells control stomatal opening.
concepts.remember: CO₂ in for photosynthesis; O₂ out.
concepts.common_confusion: Stomata also lose water vapour (transpiration).

concepts.name: Guard cells
concepts.simple_answer: Two kidney-shaped guard cells surround each stoma and control its opening and closing.
concepts.example: Stomata open in light; often close in drought.
concepts.remember: Guard cells swell to open stomata.

concepts.name: Products of photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Glucose is produced first; excess is stored as starch in leaves, stems, and roots.
concepts.example: Potato stores starch in underground stem.
concepts.remember: Immediate product: glucose; storage form: starch.
concepts.common_confusion: Starch test uses iodine — blue-black colour.

concepts.name: Activity 5.2 — starch test in leaf
concepts.simple_answer: Boil leaf in water, then alcohol, add iodine — green leaf turns blue-black showing starch from photosynthesis.
concepts.example: Variegated leaf: only green parts turn blue-black.
concepts.remember: Starch present where chlorophyll and light were available.
concepts.common_confusion: Heat leaf in water first to kill cells and soften.

concepts.name: Conditions for photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis needs light, chlorophyll, CO₂, and suitable temperature.
concepts.example: Plant in dark fails starch test — no photosynthesis.
concepts.remember: Remove any one factor → rate drops or stops.
concepts.common_confusion: Light-dependent and light-independent stages (detail optional).

concepts.name: Significance of photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis provides food for nearly all life and releases O₂ into the atmosphere.
concepts.example: All food chains start with autotrophs.
concepts.remember: Ultimate source of energy for most ecosystems.

concepts.name: Site of photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis occurs in the green parts of plants, especially leaves.
concepts.example: Non-green stems with chlorophyll also photosynthesise.
concepts.common_confusion: Roots do not photosynthesise — no chlorophyll, no light.

concepts.name: Light reaction (overview)
concepts.simple_answer: Light energy splits water; O₂ is released; energy stored temporarily in molecules.
concepts.example: O₂ bubbles from aquatic plants in bright light.
concepts.remember: Needs light; happens in grana of chloroplast.
concepts.common_confusion: Detailed biochemistry beyond Class 10 scope.

concepts.name: Dark reaction (overview)
concepts.simple_answer: CO₂ is fixed into glucose using energy from light reaction — does not require light directly.
concepts.example: Calvin cycle idea at textbook level.
concepts.remember: Can proceed in dark if products of light stage available.
concepts.common_confusion: Called 'dark' because it doesn't need light directly.

concepts.name: Factors affecting photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Rate depends on light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature, and chlorophyll amount.
concepts.example: Greenhouse farmers enrich CO₂ to boost yield.
concepts.remember: Limiting factor: the factor in shortest supply caps rate.

concepts.name: Nutrition in non-green plants
concepts.simple_answer: Some plants lack chlorophyll (e.g. Cuscuta) and are parasitic — heterotrophic nutrition.
concepts.example: Amarbel (Cuscuta) wraps around host plant.

concepts.name: Insectivorous plants
concepts.simple_answer: Plants like pitcher plant supplement minerals by trapping insects — still autotrophic for energy.
concepts.example: Pitcher plant digests insect for nitrogen.
concepts.remember: Photosynthesise but catch insects for soil-poor habitats.

concepts.name: Activity 5.3 — stomata observation
concepts.simple_answer: Peel lower epidermis of leaf, stain with safranin, observe stomata under microscope.
concepts.example: See guard cells and stomatal pore.
concepts.remember: Lower epidermis peel shows stomata clearly.
concepts.common_confusion: Safranin stains nuclei pink.

concepts.name: Gas exchange day and night
concepts.simple_answer: Day: photosynthesis dominates — CO₂ in, O₂ out. Night: only respiration — O₂ in, CO₂ out.
concepts.example: Net O₂ release only when photosynthesis > respiration.
concepts.remember: Both processes occur in plants; balance shifts.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not say plants don't respire.

concepts.name: Replenish atmosphere O₂
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis by green plants continuously replenishes atmospheric oxygen.
concepts.example: Amazon and all forests contribute O₂ globally.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis vs nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Photosynthesis is the specific autotrophic process; nutrition is the broader obtaining and use of food.
concepts.example: Photosynthesis makes food; nutrition includes using it.

concepts.name: Heterotrophic nutrition — recap
concepts.simple_answer: Organisms that cannot make their own food ingest complex organic matter and break it down.
concepts.example: Cow (herbivore), lion (carnivore), human (omnivore).
concepts.remember: All depend on autotrophs directly or indirectly.

concepts.name: Steps in holozoic nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Ingestion → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion.
concepts.example: Undigested food leaves as faeces (egestion).
concepts.common_confusion: Absorption is into blood; assimilation is use by cells.

concepts.name: Ingestion
concepts.simple_answer: Ingestion is taking food into the body through the mouth.
concepts.example: Biting and chewing apple pieces.
concepts.remember: Mouth is start of alimentary canal.

concepts.name: Digestion — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Digestion breaks complex insoluble food into simple soluble molecules using enzymes.
concepts.example: Starch → maltose → glucose.
concepts.common_confusion: Physical digestion (chewing) + chemical (enzymes).

concepts.name: Absorption
concepts.simple_answer: Absorption is uptake of digested food from intestine into blood.
concepts.example: Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries.
concepts.common_confusion: Villi increase surface area for absorption.

concepts.name: Assimilation
concepts.simple_answer: Assimilation is using absorbed nutrients for energy, growth, and repair.
concepts.example: Glucose oxidised in cells for ATP.
concepts.remember: Food becomes part of body or fuel.

concepts.name: Egestion
concepts.simple_answer: Egestion removes undigested food as faeces — not the same as excretion.
concepts.example: Fibre leaves body via anus.
concepts.remember: Egestion = undigested food out; excretion = metabolic waste.
concepts.common_confusion: Faeces are not metabolic wastes.

concepts.name: Single-chambered vs multi-chambered stomach
concepts.simple_answer: Ruminants (cow) have four-chambered stomach; humans have one stomach.
concepts.example: Cow regurgitates cud for re-chewing.
concepts.remember: Cellulose digestion needs symbiotic bacteria in ruminants.

concepts.name: Amoeba nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Amoeba extends pseudopodia around food, forms food vacuole, digests with enzymes.
concepts.example: Food vacuole fuses with lysosomes.

concepts.name: Paramoecium nutrition
concepts.simple_answer: Paramoecium has oral groove and gullet leading to food vacuole for digestion.
concepts.example: Cilia sweep food into oral groove.
concepts.remember: Specialised structures for feeding in one cell.

concepts.name: Human digestive system overview
concepts.simple_answer: Alimentary canal plus associated glands form the human digestive system.
concepts.example: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → anus.

concepts.name: Mouth and buccal cavity
concepts.simple_answer: Teeth mechanically break food; tongue mixes and tastes; saliva begins chemical digestion.
concepts.example: Chewing increases surface area for enzymes.
concepts.remember: Incisors cut, canines tear, molars grind.

concepts.name: Saliva and salivary amylase
concepts.simple_answer: Saliva moistens food and contains amylase (ptyalin) that starts starch digestion to maltose.
concepts.example: Bread tastes sweet if chewed long — maltose forms.
concepts.common_confusion: Amylase inactive in strong acid of stomach.

concepts.name: Oesophagus (food pipe)
concepts.simple_answer: Peristaltic movements push food from mouth to stomach through the oesophagus.
concepts.example: You can swallow upside down — peristalsis works.
concepts.common_confusion: Peristalsis is involuntary muscle contraction.

concepts.name: Stomach structure
concepts.simple_answer: Stomach is a muscular bag; gastric glands secrete HCl, mucus, and pepsin.
concepts.example: HCl kills bacteria and gives acid pH for pepsin.
concepts.remember: Churning mixes food with gastric juice.

concepts.name: Pepsin action
concepts.simple_answer: Pepsin breaks proteins into peptides in acidic medium of stomach.
concepts.example: Inactive pepsinogen activated by HCl.
concepts.common_confusion: Pepsin works only in acid — not in mouth.

concepts.name: Mucus in stomach
concepts.simple_answer: Mucus protects stomach lining from being digested by its own acid and pepsin.
concepts.example: Ulcers may occur if mucus layer damaged.

concepts.name: Small intestine — main digestion site
concepts.simple_answer: Complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats occurs in small intestine.
concepts.example: Receives bile and pancreatic juice.

concepts.name: Liver and bile
concepts.simple_answer: Liver makes bile stored in gall bladder; bile emulsifies fats (no enzyme).
concepts.example: Bile breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets.
concepts.common_confusion: Bile is alkaline — neutralises stomach acid.

concepts.name: Pancreatic juice
concepts.simple_answer: Pancreas secretes trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats), and pancreatic amylase (starch).
concepts.example: Juice released into duodenum.

concepts.name: Intestinal juice (succus entericus)
concepts.simple_answer: Intestinal glands secrete enzymes completing digestion of all major food types.
concepts.example: Maltase converts maltose to glucose.
concepts.remember: Carbohydrates → glucose; proteins → amino acids; fats → fatty acids + glycerol.

concepts.name: Villi and microvilli
concepts.simple_answer: Inner wall of small intestine has finger-like villi with microvilli to absorb digested food.
concepts.example: Each villus has blood capillaries and lacteal.
concepts.remember: Huge surface area in folded wall.
concepts.common_confusion: Lacteal absorbs fatty acids and glycerol.

concepts.name: Absorption in small intestine
concepts.simple_answer: Glucose and amino acids enter blood; fatty acids enter lacteals of lymph system.
concepts.example: Blood carries sugars and amino acids to liver.

concepts.name: Large intestine role
concepts.simple_answer: Large intestine absorbs water and minerals; forms and stores faeces.
concepts.example: Diarrhoea if water not reabsorbed properly.
concepts.common_confusion: No significant digestion in large intestine.

concepts.name: Rectum and anus
concepts.simple_answer: Faeces stored in rectum and eliminated through anus — egestion.
concepts.example: Defecation is egestion, not excretion.
concepts.remember: Anus is exit for undigested residue.

concepts.name: Digestive enzymes summary
concepts.simple_answer: Amylase (starch), pepsin/trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats) — know source and product.
concepts.example: Draw table: enzyme, source, substrate, product.
concepts.common_confusion: One enzyme generally acts on one substrate type.

concepts.name: pH and enzyme action
concepts.simple_answer: Salivary amylase needs neutral pH; pepsin needs acid; intestinal enzymes need alkaline pH.
concepts.example: Bicarbonate in pancreatic juice neutralises acid.
concepts.remember: Each enzyme works best at specific pH.

concepts.name: Dental hygiene
concepts.simple_answer: Brushing removes food particles; prevents acid from bacteria decaying teeth.
concepts.example: Saliva washes teeth; bacteria cause cavities.
concepts.remember: Prevention is part of nutrition health.

concepts.name: Disorders — indigestion
concepts.simple_answer: Indigestion from inadequate enzyme action or overeating; antacids neutralise excess acid.
concepts.example: Antacids raise pH in stomach.

concepts.name: Human digestion summary
concepts.simple_answer: Mouth (starch start) → stomach (protein start) → small intestine (complete digestion + absorption).
concepts.example: Trace one bite of bread to glucose in blood.
concepts.remember: Know organ order and main function each.

concepts.name: Respiration — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Respiration is the process of releasing energy from food (glucose) inside cells.
concepts.example: ATP powers muscle contraction.
concepts.remember: Not the same as breathing — breathing is ventilation.
concepts.common_confusion: Breathing ≠ respiration.

concepts.name: Why respiration is essential
concepts.simple_answer: Energy from respiration drives synthesis, transport, movement, and maintenance.
concepts.example: Nerve impulses need ATP constantly.

concepts.name: Breathing vs respiration
concepts.simple_answer: Breathing ( ventilation) is inhaling/exhaling air; respiration is biochemical breakdown of glucose in cells.
concepts.example: Lungs move air; mitochondria release energy.
concepts.remember: Breathing provides O₂ for cellular respiration.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often conflate the two terms.

concepts.name: Glucose as fuel
concepts.simple_answer: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is the common substrate broken down in respiration to release energy.
concepts.example: From digested carbohydrates.
concepts.remember: Fats and proteins can also be respired.

concepts.name: ATP — energy currency
concepts.simple_answer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) stores and transfers energy for cellular work.
concepts.example: Muscle uses ATP for contraction.
concepts.remember: Energy released when ATP → ADP + Pi.

concepts.name: Aerobic respiration — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and completely breaks glucose into CO₂, water, and much ATP.
concepts.example: Occurs in mitochondria of cells.
concepts.remember: Maximum energy from one glucose molecule.
concepts.common_confusion: Needs continuous O₂ supply.

concepts.name: Anaerobic respiration — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Anaerobic respiration breaks glucose without oxygen, producing less energy and different products.
concepts.example: Yeast: ethanol + CO₂. Muscles: lactic acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Also called fermentation in yeast.

concepts.name: Respiration in plants
concepts.simple_answer: Plant cells respire all the time in mitochondria — roots, stems, leaves, flowers.
concepts.example: Germinating seeds respire vigorously.
concepts.remember: Photosynthesis and respiration both occur in plants.
concepts.common_confusion: Plants do not 'only photosynthesise'.

concepts.name: Gas exchange in plants
concepts.simple_answer: Plants exchange O₂ and CO₂ through stomata and lenticels; roots also need O₂ in soil air spaces.
concepts.example: Waterlogged soil kills roots — no O₂ for respiration.
concepts.remember: Stomata for leaves; lenticels for woody stems.

concepts.name: Respiration chapter map
concepts.simple_answer: Aerobic in mitochondria; anaerobic in cytoplasm (and yeast); compare energy yield next days.
concepts.example: Activity 5.1 demonstrates yeast anaerobic respiration.

concepts.name: Aerobic respiration steps (overview)
concepts.simple_answer: Glycolysis in cytoplasm → pyruvate enters mitochondria → complete oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O.
concepts.example: Pyruvate breakdown needs O₂ in mitochondria.
concepts.common_confusion: Krebs cycle detail optional for Class 10.

concepts.name: Glycolysis
concepts.simple_answer: One glucose molecule splits into two pyruvate molecules in cytoplasm, releasing small amount of ATP.
concepts.example: Does not require oxygen directly.
concepts.remember: Common to aerobic and anaerobic paths.

concepts.name: Mitochondria — powerhouse
concepts.simple_answer: Mitochondria are organelles where pyruvate is fully oxidised in presence of O₂ to release maximum ATP.
concepts.example: Muscle cells have many mitochondria.
concepts.remember: Pyruvate + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + ATP in mitochondria.
concepts.common_confusion: More mitochondria = more aerobic capacity.

concepts.name: Products of aerobic respiration
concepts.simple_answer: CO₂, water, and about 38 ATP molecules (theoretical max) per glucose.
concepts.example: CO₂ leaves body via lungs.

concepts.name: Respiration in humans — overview
concepts.simple_answer: O₂ inhaled → diffuses into blood → carried to cells → used in mitochondria; CO₂ reverse path.
concepts.example: Haemoglobin carries O₂ in RBCs.

concepts.name: Alveoli structure
concepts.simple_answer: Alveoli are tiny air sacs in lungs with thin moist walls and rich blood capillaries for gas exchange.
concepts.example: Millions of alveoli = huge surface area.
concepts.remember: Thin wall + moisture + capillaries = efficient diffusion.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse alveoli with nephron.

concepts.name: Diffusion in alveoli
concepts.simple_answer: O₂ diffuses from alveolar air into blood; CO₂ diffuses from blood into alveoli to be exhaled.

visual.label: O₂ in, CO₂ out at alveoli

concepts.example: Steep concentration gradient maintained by blood flow.

concepts.name: Haemoglobin and O₂ transport
concepts.simple_answer: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds O₂ in lungs and releases it in tissues.
concepts.example: Oxyhaemoglobin forms in lungs.
concepts.remember: Iron in haemoglobin binds O₂ reversibly.

concepts.name: Activity 5.1 — yeast and sugar
concepts.simple_answer: Yeast in sugar solution produces CO₂ bubbles — anaerobic respiration (fermentation).
concepts.example: Balloon on flask inflates with CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Same activity shows gas evolution sign of life.

concepts.name: Comparing energy yield
concepts.simple_answer: Aerobic respiration releases far more ATP per glucose than anaerobic fermentation.
concepts.why: Why O₂ is vital for active animals.
concepts.example: Sprinters feel burn — temporary anaerobic in muscles.
concepts.remember: Aerobic is preferred when O₂ available.

concepts.name: Anaerobic in yeast
concepts.simple_answer: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol, CO₂, and limited ATP — used in bread and brewing.
concepts.example: Bread rises from CO₂ bubbles in dough.

concepts.name: Anaerobic in muscle cells
concepts.simple_answer: During intense exercise, muscles respire anaerobically producing lactic acid and less ATP.
concepts.example: Cramp and fatigue from lactic acid accumulation.
concepts.remember: Temporary when O₂ delivery lags demand.
concepts.common_confusion: Oxygen debt repaid after exercise.

concepts.name: Oxygen debt
concepts.simple_answer: After vigorous exercise, extra O₂ needed to oxidise accumulated lactic acid — breathing stays heavy.
concepts.example: Deep breathing clears lactic acid.

concepts.name: Aerobic vs anaerobic — table
concepts.simple_answer: Aerobic: needs O₂, CO₂ + H₂O products, more ATP, in mitochondria. Anaerobic: no O₂, partial products, less ATP, cytoplasm.
concepts.example: Fill table for location, O₂, products, ATP.
concepts.remember: Know at least two differences each.
concepts.common_confusion: Photosynthesis is not respiration reversed in location.

concepts.name: When anaerobic is used
concepts.simple_answer: Anaerobic pathways when O₂ supply insufficient — yeast in sealed flask, sprinting muscles.
concepts.example: Root cells in waterlogged soil may switch.
concepts.remember: Survival pathway, not primary for humans.

concepts.name: Respiration vs photosynthesis
concepts.simple_answer: Respiration breaks glucose for energy in all living cells; photosynthesis makes glucose in green plants using light.
concepts.example: Both involve gas exchange but opposite roles overall in plants.
concepts.remember: Respiration: all cells. Photosynthesis: chloroplasts only.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not swap equations or locations.

concepts.name: Balancing photosynthesis and respiration
concepts.simple_answer: Plants produce O₂ by photosynthesis and use O₂ in respiration — net gas exchange varies.
concepts.example: Young plant in light releases net O₂.
concepts.remember: Both processes run in green plants.

concepts.name: Respiration in germinating seeds
concepts.simple_answer: Seeds respire actively during germination even before green shoots appear.
concepts.example: Warm flask with seeds — heat from respiration.

concepts.name: Commercial fermentation
concepts.simple_answer: Anaerobic yeast respiration used for bread, beer, wine, and bioethanol production.
concepts.example: CO₂ raises dough; ethanol in beverages.

concepts.name: Respiration summary
concepts.simple_answer: All living cells respire; aerobic in mitochondria is main path; anaerobic when O₂ limited.
concepts.example: Link breathing → blood → cell → mitochondria.
concepts.remember: Draw full pathway for exam revision.

concepts.name: Transport in plants — why needed
concepts.simple_answer: Plants need transport to move water, minerals, and food between roots, stem, and leaves.
concepts.example: Tall trees move water 50+ metres up.
concepts.remember: Roots absorb; leaves photosynthesise — connection needed.

concepts.name: Xylem — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from roots upward to all plant parts.
concepts.example: Dead hollow cells form continuous tubes.
concepts.common_confusion: Xylem carries water — not food.

concepts.name: Phloem — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Phloem transports food (sucrose) from leaves to storage organs and growing parts.
concepts.example: Bark contains phloem; peeling ring kills tree.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not swap xylem and phloem functions.

concepts.name: Root hair cells
concepts.simple_answer: Root hairs increase surface area to absorb water and minerals from soil by osmosis and active uptake.
concepts.example: Millions of root hairs near tip.
concepts.remember: Large surface area in small zone.

concepts.name: Path of water in plant
concepts.simple_answer: Soil water → root hair → xylem → stem → leaves → evaporates from stomata.
concepts.example: Activity 5.4 shows coloured water in xylem.

concepts.name: Transpiration
concepts.simple_answer: Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial parts of plant, mainly through stomata.
concepts.example: Wilting on hot dry day.
concepts.common_confusion: Transpiration cools leaf surface.

concepts.name: Transpiration pull
concepts.simple_answer: Evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water column up through xylem.
concepts.example: Like sucking drink through straw.
concepts.remember: No energy spent by plant to lift water — passive pull.

concepts.name: Activity 5.4 — xylem dye experiment
concepts.simple_answer: Place plant stem in eosin/coloured water; cut sections show dye in xylem vessels.
concepts.example: Red streaks in stem cross-section.
concepts.remember: Dye follows water pathway in xylem.

concepts.name: Activity 5.5 — transpiration bag
concepts.simple_answer: Plastic bag on leaf shows water droplets inside — proof of transpiration.
concepts.example: Bag mists up over hours in sun.

concepts.name: Xylem tissue structure
concepts.simple_answer: Xylem has vessels and tracheids — thick lignified walls, no cytoplasm in mature cells.
concepts.example: Lignin strengthens against suction.

concepts.name: Phloem tissue structure
concepts.simple_answer: Phloem has sieve tubes and companion cells; living cells transport dissolved sugars.
concepts.example: Companion cells help load sugar.
concepts.remember: Sieve plates allow flow between cells.

concepts.name: Translocation
concepts.simple_answer: Translocation is movement of food (sucrose) through phloem from source to sink.
concepts.example: Leaves (source) → roots/t fruits (sink).
concepts.common_confusion: Bidirectional — up or down as needed.

concepts.name: Source and sink
concepts.simple_answer: Source is where food is made/stored for export; sink is where food is used or stored.
concepts.example: Leaf in summer = source; growing root = sink.
concepts.remember: Direction reverses seasonally in some plants.

concepts.name: Ringing experiment
concepts.simple_answer: Removing phloem ring around trunk causes swelling above cut — food cannot pass down.
concepts.example: Tree may die if bark ring removed completely.

concepts.name: Xylem vs phloem summary
concepts.simple_answer: Xylem: water + minerals, upward, dead cells. Phloem: food, bidirectional, living sieve tubes.
concepts.example: Never swap contents or direction.
concepts.remember: Both are vascular tissues in plants.
concepts.common_confusion: Xylem/phloem swap is top misconception.

concepts.name: Transport in aquatic plants
concepts.simple_answer: Some aquatic plants have reduced xylem support; still need gas and nutrient transport.
concepts.example: Hydrilla releases O₂ bubbles in water.

concepts.name: Mineral uptake
concepts.simple_answer: Minerals enter root hairs by active transport against concentration gradient — needs energy.
concepts.why: Not passive like some water entry.
concepts.example: Nitrates for proteins; magnesium for chlorophyll.
concepts.remember: Active transport uses ATP from respiration.

concepts.name: Wilting and recovery
concepts.simple_answer: Excess transpiration without water uptake causes wilting; watering restores turgor.
concepts.example: Hot afternoon wilting; evening recovery.

concepts.name: Guard cells and transpiration
concepts.simple_answer: Open stomata allow CO₂ for photosynthesis but increase transpiration water loss.
concepts.why: Balance gas gain vs water loss.
concepts.example: Desert plants have sunken stomata.

concepts.name: Plant transport summary
concepts.simple_answer: Xylem + transpiration pull for water up; phloem + translocation for food to all parts.
concepts.example: Draw whole plant with both pathways labelled.

concepts.name: Transport in animals — need
concepts.simple_answer: Animals need circulatory system to deliver O₂, food, hormones and remove wastes from all cells.
concepts.example: Human has ~5 litres blood circulating.
concepts.remember: Diffusion alone fails beyond tiny thickness.

concepts.name: Blood — components
concepts.simple_answer: Blood has plasma (liquid) and formed elements: RBCs, WBCs, and platelets.
concepts.example: Plasma is straw-coloured, mostly water.
concepts.remember: RBCs carry O₂; WBCs fight infection; platelets clot.

concepts.name: Plasma function
concepts.simple_answer: Plasma transports digested food, CO₂, hormones, and waste products dissolved in water.
concepts.example: Urea carried in plasma to kidney.

concepts.name: Red blood cells
concepts.simple_answer: RBCs contain haemoglobin; biconcave shape increases surface area; no nucleus in mature human RBC.
concepts.example: Millions per drop of blood.

concepts.name: White blood cells
concepts.simple_answer: WBCs defend against pathogens; larger, have nucleus, can leave blood vessels.
concepts.example: Phagocytes engulf bacteria.

concepts.name: Platelets
concepts.simple_answer: Platelets are cell fragments that help blood clot at injury sites.
concepts.example: Cut finger stops bleeding from clot.

concepts.name: Blood vessels — three types
concepts.simple_answer: Arteries carry blood away from heart; veins return blood to heart; capillaries exchange with tissues.
concepts.example: Arteries thick-walled; veins have valves.

concepts.name: Arteries vs veins
concepts.simple_answer: Arteries: thick elastic walls, high pressure, no valves. Veins: thinner walls, valves prevent backflow.
concepts.example: Aorta is largest artery.
concepts.remember: Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — exception.

concepts.name: Capillaries
concepts.simple_answer: Capillaries connect arteries to veins; thin walls allow exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes.
concepts.example: Blood slows in capillary beds.

concepts.name: Double circulation preview
concepts.simple_answer: Human heart drives double circulation — pulmonary and systemic circuits.
concepts.example: Blood passes heart twice per full body circuit.
concepts.remember: Separates low-pressure lung circuit from high-pressure body.

concepts.name: Human heart — chambers
concepts.simple_answer: Heart has four chambers: two atria (receive blood) and two ventricles (pump blood out).
concepts.example: Left side pumps to body; right to lungs.

concepts.name: Pulmonary circulation
concepts.simple_answer: Right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs; returns oxygenated to left atrium.
concepts.example: Pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein.

concepts.name: Systemic circulation
concepts.simple_answer: Left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to entire body; returns deoxygenated to right atrium.
concepts.example: Aorta branches to all organs.
concepts.remember: Left ventricle wall is thickest — high pressure.

concepts.name: Heart valves
concepts.simple_answer: Valves prevent backflow — tricuspid, bicuspid (mitral), pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves.
concepts.example: Valves snap shut after ventricle contraction.

concepts.name: Heartbeat mechanism
concepts.simple_answer: SA node triggers rhythmic contraction — atria contract then ventricles ( lub-dub ).
concepts.example: Activity 5.6 — stethoscope on chest.

concepts.name: Activity 5.6 — heartbeat sound
concepts.simple_answer: Stethoscope on chest hears lub-dub of valves closing during cardiac cycle.
concepts.example: Lub = AV valves close; dub = semilunar close.
concepts.remember: Count beats per minute at rest.

concepts.name: Pulse rate
concepts.simple_answer: Pulse is wave of arterial expansion felt at wrist; equals heart rate at rest.
concepts.example: Normal resting pulse ~70–80 bpm in adults.

concepts.name: Activity 5.7 — pulse after exercise
concepts.simple_answer: Pulse rate increases after exercise because muscles need more O₂ and glucose faster.
concepts.example: Compare resting vs after running.
concepts.remember: Heart pumps faster to meet demand.

concepts.name: Lymphatic system (brief)
concepts.simple_answer: Lymph carries absorbed fats from intestine and returns tissue fluid to blood.
concepts.example: Lymph nodes filter pathogens.

concepts.name: Circulation summary
concepts.simple_answer: Heart → arteries → capillaries → veins → heart; O₂ and food delivered, CO₂ and wastes collected.
concepts.example: Trace one red blood cell through full circuit.
concepts.remember: Double circulation in humans and birds.

concepts.name: Excretion — definition
concepts.simple_answer: Excretion is removal of harmful metabolic wastes produced in the body.
concepts.example: Urea from protein metabolism.
concepts.remember: Not the same as egestion or sweating alone.
concepts.common_confusion: Excretion removes metabolic wastes.

concepts.name: Egestion vs excretion vs secretion
concepts.simple_answer: Egestion: undigested food out. Excretion: metabolic waste out. Secretion: useful substances released.
concepts.example: Faeces = egestion; urine = excretion.

concepts.name: Excretion in plants
concepts.simple_answer: Plants excrete O₂ (photosynthesis), CO₂ (respiration), water vapour, and store or drop wastes.
concepts.example: Plants store waste in vacuoles or bark.
concepts.remember: Resins and gums are waste products.
concepts.common_confusion: Plants don't have kidneys.

concepts.name: Plant waste removal methods
concepts.simple_answer: Plants lose gaseous wastes through stomata; shed leaves; store wastes in cellular vacuoles and old xylem.
concepts.example: Tamarind stores tartaric acid in fruits.
concepts.remember: Guttation exudes liquid water with salts.

concepts.name: Excretion in humans — organs
concepts.simple_answer: Main excretory organs: kidneys (urine), lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat — some urea/salts).
concepts.example: Kidneys primary for nitrogenous waste.

concepts.name: Kidney location and role
concepts.simple_answer: Pair of kidneys filter blood to remove urea, excess water, and salts as urine.
concepts.example: Kidneys maintain water-salt balance (osmoregulation).
concepts.common_confusion: Kidneys → excretion, not digestion.

concepts.name: Urine pathway
concepts.simple_answer: Kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra.
concepts.example: Bladder stores urine temporarily.

concepts.name: Structure of kidney (overview)
concepts.simple_answer: Kidney has outer cortex and inner medulla containing millions of nephrons.
concepts.example: Renal artery brings blood; renal vein takes filtered blood.

concepts.name: Why excretion matters
concepts.simple_answer: Accumulated wastes poison cells — urea must be removed to maintain homeostasis.
concepts.example: Kidney failure raises blood urea dangerously.

concepts.name: Excretion block preview
concepts.simple_answer: Day 16 covers nephron structure, filtration, and Activity 5.8 dialysis model.
concepts.example: Do not confuse alveoli (gas) with nephron (filter).
concepts.remember: Nephron is functional unit of kidney.

concepts.name: Nephron — functional unit
concepts.simple_answer: Nephron is the structural and functional unit of kidney — filters blood and forms urine.
concepts.example: Each kidney has about 1 million nephrons.
concepts.common_confusion: Alveoli vs nephron is common confusion.

concepts.name: Nephron parts
concepts.simple_answer: Nephron: Bowman's capsule + glomerulus, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct.
concepts.example: Glomerulus is capillary knot for filtration.
concepts.remember: Know at least four parts for exam.

concepts.name: Ultrafiltration in glomerulus
concepts.simple_answer: Blood pressure forces water, urea, glucose, salts into Bowman's capsule; large proteins stay in blood.
concepts.example: Filterate enters tubule.

concepts.name: Reabsorption in tubule
concepts.simple_answer: Useful substances (glucose, most water, salts) reabsorbed into blood; waste stays in tubule.
concepts.example: All glucose normally reabsorbed.

concepts.name: Urine formation
concepts.simple_answer: Remaining fluid in collecting duct is urine — concentrated urea, excess water and salts.
concepts.example: Urine ~95% water.

concepts.name: Activity 5.8 — dialysis model
concepts.simple_answer: Visking tubing in water bath models selective permeability like dialysis in kidney failure treatment.
concepts.example: Small molecules pass through membrane; starch/protein retained.

concepts.name: Kidney failure and dialysis
concepts.simple_answer: When kidneys fail, dialysis machine removes urea from blood using semi-permeable membrane.
concepts.example: Regular dialysis replaces kidney function.

concepts.name: NCERT summary — life processes
concepts.simple_answer: Nutrition, respiration, transport, and excretion maintain life in plants and animals.
concepts.example: Match process to organ system.

concepts.name: Must-know comparisons
concepts.simple_answer: Autotroph vs heterotroph; aerobic vs anaerobic; xylem vs phloem; breathing vs respiration; egestion vs excretion.
concepts.example: One table each for top five pairs.

concepts.name: Unit 1 complete
concepts.simple_answer: Unit 1 Life Processes complete — 160 concept cards; proceed to Practice when unlocked.
concepts.example: 200 MCQs in bank; Stage 2 days 17–20 follow.
